steps.title: Wanted: A Toy That Jumps!
steps.story: Leila's favourite toy shop wants a brand-new toy for its window, a little grasshopper that really jumps. The owner has one rule: no batteries and no motors. Can YOU build a toy that stores up energy and jumps as high as possible?

steps.prompt: Do you already have an idea for a toy that jumps all by itself?

steps.intro: How does nature store energy to jump? Some tiny animals jump far higher than their muscles alone could push them. Let's find out their secret!

clues.text: A flea is only about 2 mm long, but it can jump over 100 times its own length. It squashes a pad of super-springy stuff called resilin, holds it with a catch, then lets it snap.
A kangaroo's back legs have long, springy tendons. Each time it lands, the tendons stretch and store energy, then spring back to push it into the next hop.
A click beetle lying on its back bends its body and locks it with a peg. When the peg slips, the body snaps straight with a loud click and flips the beetle into the air.
A frog sits with its long back legs folded up tight. When it jumps, the legs unfold into long levers, and springy tendons help fling it far forward.

steps.secret: Load, lock, release! Muscles push slowly, but a spring can let go all at once. So nature's jumpers slowly squash or stretch something springy, hold it with a catch, then let it go in a flash. All the stored energy comes out in one quick burst. Engineers call this a latch, and it is used in toys, catapults and some tiny jumping robots.
steps.reveal_hint: What springy part will your toy load up, and what will hold it until the jump?

steps.instructions: Make a jumping card: cut 2 rectangles of card (about 5 cm by 8 cm), cut a small notch at each end, and join them with a rubber band hooked through the notches. Fold them flat together, put them on the table and let go. Measure how high they pop against a ruler or a tape measure stuck to the wall. Try a thin band, a thick band and two thin bands. Point the card away from faces.
hints: Use the same card and the same table for every test, and only change the rubber band. That keeps the test fair.
A band that is stretched more stores more energy. If your card only wobbles, make the notches further apart so the band is tighter.

steps.prompt: Draw your grasshopper toy loaded and ready to jump.
steps.guidance: Label the springy part that stores energy, the catch that holds it, and how you release it. Add an arrow for which way it will jump.

steps.instructions: Build a grasshopper toy from card, lolly sticks, rubber bands, paper clips and tape. Give it a springy part, a catch to hold it loaded, and a way to release it without pushing. Stand a tape measure against a wall and jump it 3 times. Ask an adult to help with cutting, and never aim it at anyone's face.
test_criteria: What is the highest jump in cm out of your 3 tries?
Does your grasshopper land on its feet?
Improve one thing and test again. Did it jump higher?
hints: If your toy jumps sideways, the spring is pulling off-centre. Put the rubber band right in the middle.
Load it slowly, lock it with a paper tab or a bent paper clip, then pull the tab. A clean, sudden release gives the biggest jump.

steps.celebration_text: Your grasshopper leaps in the shop window, and a crowd of kids is cheering it on! No batteries needed.
steps.share_prompt: Share a photo of your jumping toy and your highest jump on the Ideas Wall. Which nature jumper did you copy?

age_tier_variants.summary: Test rubber bands on a jumping card, then build a grasshopper toy that loads, locks and releases energy to jump as high as possible.
Explain elastic potential energy and power amplification with a latch, measure jump height against band stretch, and compare your toy with flea resilin and kangaroo tendons.
